title: What are the tyre strategy options for the Mexico City GP?
excerpt:
You might think a man with 104 pole positions would not be too excited about one more, but Lewis Hamilton – never one to hide his mood – was bouncing up and down with joy at the conclusion of Qualifying yesterday, much like he did 20 seasons ago, when bagging his first.

No.105 has been a long time coming. His first for Ferrari, three years and a team change after his last for Mercedes.

The good news for Hamilton in his quest for victory is that practice suggested overtaking in Sunday's race is going to be very difficult. The bad news is that it’s an awfully long way to Turn 1, and he’s going to be towing a pack of highly motivated rivals all the way down to the braking point.

George Russell starts P2, with Charles Leclerc and Kimi Antonelli on the second row, while Max Verstappen and Lando Norris are on row three. They’re all winners this season, and while Antonelli has reason to be a little more circumspect, the others are here to add to their tally. The race is tantalisingly poised between one stop and two, which is going to make it very interesting indeed.

title: How F1 drivers and teams have embraced Dia de Muertos
excerpt:
The Mexico City Grand Prix is renowned for its passionate crowds, colourful paddock and spectacular celebrations. But this year, the race takes place during one of Mexico's most important cultural occasions – Dia de Muertos, or Day of the Dead.

Taking place around the beginning of November, Dia de Muertos is a time for families to remember loved ones who have passed away and is traditionally marked through decorated altars, food, flowers and celebrations that bring communities together.

For Formula 1, the celebration has become a familiar part of its annual visit to the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez. Drivers have embraced the occasion through special helmets, elaborate face paint and even cooking challenges, while the paddock has welcomed performers and displays inspired by Mexican traditions.

As the 2026 race weekend coincides with Dia de Muertos, here's a closer look at the celebration, the meanings behind its most recognisable customs and how they have made their mark on F1.

What is Dia de Muertos?

Although its name might suggest otherwise, Dia de Muertos is as much a celebration of life as it is a remembrance of death. Rooted in pre-Hispanic traditions that later became intertwined with Catholic observances introduced by the Spanish, the celebration centres on the belief that deceased loved ones can temporarily return to the world of the living. While customs differ between communities, 1 November is commonly associated with remembering children who have passed, while 2 November is dedicated to deceased adults.

Rather than being an occasion solely for mourning, Dia de Muertos provides families with an opportunity to reconnect with those they have lost through their favourite foods, personal belongings and shared memories. Homes and cemeteries are typically decorated with flowers, candles and offerings, while relatives gather to celebrate the lives of their loved ones. Its cultural significance was recognised by UNESCO when the tradition was proclaimed in 2003, before being inscribed on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2008.

When Dia de Muertos inspires the drivers' helmets

Special helmets have become a regular feature of the Mexico City Grand Prix, with drivers using the occasion to incorporate Mexican artwork into their designs.

In 2024, Carlos Sainz unveiled a Dia de Muertos-inspired helmet featuring a colourful skull motif across the crown. The design also incorporated a chilli pepper, referencing his long-standing nickname. The Spaniard went on to win the race for Ferrari, making it a memorable helmet for his collection.

Sainz was not the only driver incorporating the occasion into his race weekend that year, with Pierre Gasly also opting for a special design featuring Dia de Muertos-inspired imagery. However, few drivers have embraced Mexican heritage through their helmet designs as consistently as Sergio Perez.

For his home race in 2022, the Red Bull driver unveiled a design featuring La Catrina, an elegantly dressed skeletal figure who has become one of the most recognisable symbols associated with the festivities. The helmet also incorporated papel picado, the decorative paper banners traditionally created by cutting intricate patterns into sheets of coloured tissue paper.

La Catrina has a fascinating history of her own. The figure emerged through the work of Mexican printmaker Jose Guadalupe Posada, whose satirical skeletal imagery was later popularised by the artist Diego Rivera. Today, she appears throughout Dia de Muertos celebrations, with her distinctive hat and elaborate clothing inspiring everything from face paint to enormous public installations.

The following year, Perez unveiled another helmet created by Mexican artist Karla Lozano, whose winning design incorporated papel picado, alebrijes and other cultural references to Mexico and his home state of Jalisco. While alebrijes belong to a wider tradition of Mexican folk art, they have also become familiar sights at contemporary Dia de Muertos celebrations.

The paddock gets a Dia de Muertos makeover

Over the years, the Mexico City Grand Prix paddock has become almost as colourful as the celebrations taking place across the capital.

Anyone who remembers the 2016 Mexico City Grand Prix might recall a rather unusual appearance by Red Bull team mates Max Verstappen and Daniel Ricciardo. Arriving for their Thursday media commitments, the pair were almost unrecognisable beneath elaborate skull-inspired face paint, embracing the imagery associated with Dia de Muertos. Mercedes also joined in with the festivities that year, decorating their hospitality area to mark the occasion.

The colourful skeletal designs worn by the Red Bull drivers echoed the calavera, or skull, imagery commonly seen during Dia de Muertos. Skulls appear in various forms during Día de Muertos, including decorative artwork, face paint and sugar skulls known as calaveras de azucar.

The tradition has continued at subsequent races. In 2024, drivers entering the paddock were welcomed by performers dressed as Catrinas, who handed out cempasuchil flowers, the bright orange Mexican marigolds closely associated with Dia de Muertos. Charles Leclerc made a particularly memorable entrance in a traditional charro-style outfit associated with mariachi musicians, carrying one of the flowers given to him on arrival.

Cempasuchil flowers are traditionally used to help guide the spirits of deceased loved ones back to their families, with petals often arranged along pathways leading towards altars.

A taste of Mexico

Food is central to Dia de Muertos, and it has also provided Formula 1 drivers with some rather entertaining experiences away from the track. During the 2024 Mexico City Grand Prix weekend, Oscar Piastri swapped racing duties for food preparation, making guacamole alongside a Dia de Muertos performer in the paddock.

While guacamole itself is not specific to the celebration, food plays an important role in Dia de Muertos, with families preparing dishes enjoyed by deceased relatives and placing them on ofrendas.

These offerings vary depending on the individual being remembered and the traditions of each family, with everything from tamales and mole to fruit, sweets and favourite drinks appearing alongside photographs and personal possessions.

Perhaps the most recognisable seasonal speciality is pan de muerto, a traditional sweet bread prepared around Dia de Muertos. Often flavoured with orange blossom or citrus and topped with sugar, some versions feature dough decorations shaped to resemble bones.

Recipes differ across Mexico, with regional varieties and contemporary fillings adding to the range available in bakeries during October and November. This year, the Mexico City Grand Prix organisers have confirmed that visitors will be able to sample different versions at the circuit, including traditional sugar-coated breads and filled alternatives.

Ofrendas and the meaning behind the celebrations

While the colourful costumes, special helmets and paddock activities have become familiar features of the Mexico City Grand Prix, one of the central Dia de Muertos traditions is the ofrenda.

These altars, created in homes, cemeteries and public spaces, are dedicated to deceased loved ones, bringing together photographs, personal belongings and offerings that reflect the lives of those being remembered.

For the 2026 Mexico City Grand Prix, organisers have confirmed that an altar de muertos will be installed in the circuit's Blue Zone, dedicated to members of the motorsport community who have passed away.

It marks a particularly poignant addition to this year's race weekend, offering a connection between Mexico's tradition of remembrance and the people who have helped shape the sport's history.

With the Grand Prix taking place on 1 November, the display also serves as a reminder of the significance behind the festivities that have become such a recognisable part of F1's annual visit. Beyond the elaborate artwork and celebrations, Dia de Muertos remains an occasion for honouring those who are no longer here, ensuring their memories continue to be shared.

title: ‘This experience has shaped me’ – Gasly on his work with Make-A-Wish
excerpt:
Following on from Formula 1’s first sport-wide Social Impact Report, where it was announced that more than 500,000 young people across 71 countries had benefitted from Formula 1’s charitable programmes in 2025, F1.com speaks to Alpine driver and Make-a-Wish France Ambassador Pierre Gasly about his work with the charity – with F1 having helped to make over 50 wishes come true last year for children living with critical illnesses.

One experience in particular from Gasly’s ambassadorship with the Make-A-Wish Foundation has stayed with him. The French driver was giving a tour of Alpine’s Enstone factory in the UK to a 17-year-old boy living with a critical illness.

“I took him around the factory in an Alpine A110 road car, and he could name every single car model that we crossed paths with on the road: the year, the engine, the horsepower. And I was, like, mind-blown – like, ‘I should be the car guy here and I'm clearly not!’ His knowledge about cars was insane, and he was so positive – a very bright personality… I felt pleased that I could make it happen.”

Within two months, Gasly’s guest at Alpine that day had passed away from his illness. If Gasly had been convinced of the Make-A-Wish Foundation’s worth when he became an ambassador for the charity back in 2023, it was that experience that made it hit home even more.

The Make-A-Wish Foundation’s roots run all the way back to 1979, when a seven-year-old child from Scottsdale, Arizona called Chris Greicius was diagnosed with leukaemia. With the help of his local community, Chris had his wish of being a police officer for a day granted, taking a police helicopter tour of Phoenix while wearing his own special uniform, and getting sworn in as Arizona’s first and only honorary Department of Public Safety member. And sadly, just like Gasly’s guest at Enstone, Chris would die a short time later from his cancer. The Make-a-Wish Foundation was born from Chris’ experience.

Like most young drivers coming into Formula 1, Gasly’s primary focus in his first seasons in the sport were beating his team mates and building his reputation with stand-out performances on track. But once established in the paddock, Gasly quickly realised that he wanted to start using his position to make a positive impact on the world.

“I remember having the conversation with my manager, and I told him that I'd like to find ways of giving back and actually being more involved with this sort of charity work – to just involve myself,” says Gasly. “Make-a-Wish felt like a good fit.

“I think it's a lot about trying to find ways to give back to people, thanks to the chance I have to be in the position that I am in Formula 1,” he adds. “Experiences I've had with Make-A-Wish and seeing the impact that I could have on these kids has been absolutely incredible.

“It's just very fulfilling as a human to feel that I can positively impact [these kids] – and it doesn't matter at the end of the day whether you impact one million people's lives or one, as long as I can do something positive and actually have a positive action and support someone, I find it very special.”

Gasly’s activities with the charity have ranged from auctioning off helmets to meeting kids at track, with Gasly clear that the positive impact of these meetings flows both ways.

“I would say this experience has shaped me,” he says of his ambassadorship. “I've had a fair few experiences that have made me stronger in the way that I approach and look at things.”

Formula 1 publishes first sport-wide Social Impact Report

Asked by F1.com if he ever struggles to contain his emotions when meeting these kids and hearing their stories, often just moments before jumping into his racing car, he pauses before replying: “Not to say that I don't get affected because I'm someone who is quite emotional – and at the end of the day it's definitely tough to see the reality as it is.

“But I would say it just makes you reflect quite a lot on your life, on people's lives, and the chance that we have to live in the conditions that we live in.

“Some of these kids, already from a very young age, they know that unfortunately, they won't have the same chance and they won't have same amount of time as we get. So it definitely makes you reflect on a few things in life.

“I think it’s had a real impact on my life, on appreciating everything we have. Because it's so easy to complain about small stuff but… we should not allow ourselves to complain when we see the chance that we have to live our lives.”

While Gasly’s high profile as an F1 driver is helping to raise awareness of the Make-a-Wish Foundation, the Alpine driver is adamant that everyone and anyone can contribute to help make kids’ wishes come true…

“I always say there is no small or big donation,” says Gasly. “Any donation is used for these wishes and to realise the dreams for these kids who are obviously facing unique conditions. And that's why I always encourage people to donate.

“Sometimes you think two euros, five euros, 10 euros won't make a difference, but the reality is when you're talking a hundred, or a thousand people making a five-euro donation, it does change the life of hundreds of kids.

“People also wonder, ‘Where is my donation going to go? Does it actually impact anything?’ I think in the position that I am in as an ambassador, I can say that all these donations actually go to these kids and do change their lives and impact their lives very positively.

“And when you see the impact – and I’ve had the chance to see it live, right in front of me, how beneficial it is for these kids to actually get to live an incredible moment that they've dreamed of their entire life – you just realise it's worth everything.”

title: Alonso's 'frustration is beyond imagination' after issues
excerpt:
Fernando Alonso has stated that his "frustration is beyond imagination" after a power unit problem brought the Aston Martin driver's Qualifying for the Mexico City Grand Prix to an early end.

Alonso was robbed of the chance to show what he could do by a painful power unit issue early in Q1 after what had been a reliable weekend for him up to that point, with the team explaining a suspected water pressure issue linked to the ERS system was the cause.

The Spaniard finished Friday’s Free Practice 2 session in P12, just 0.769s off the pacesetting Ferrari of Charles Leclerc, a margin that suggested that he was very much in the midfield fight.

Alonso put in a good first lap to top the times in the opening minutes of the session but then received an urgent radio message from the Aston Martin pit wall to stop the car, which he did just short of the pit lane entrance before visibly showing his frustration.

“It was 100 metres away from the garage, but probably the problem was bigger than anything possible to do in the garage," he said.

"So yeah, the safest thing for everyone else also on track was to stop – and I followed the instruction.”

Asked if he’d been optimistic after that strong Friday showing, the two-time World Champion replied with: “I was…”

However, that didn’t quite extend to a place in Q3 being a realistic possibility, although a decent result was lost.

“Probably difficult, but [in practice] we were P12, P13, P11, so we were in the window. If we put a good lap, maybe it was possible, but I think that was probably too optimistic. Maybe P13, P12 was our position today.”

Mexico has proved better suited to the AMR26 package compared to other tracks than had been anticipated, and Alonso said there was a simple reason.

"Less straights. There are two straights only into [Turn] 1, into 4. The rest, with the level of grip so low, you hardly can go full throttle, so there is less power sensitivity here. So it was maybe because of that.”

The experienced Spaniard is pessimistic about the chances of making progress from P18 on the grid at a track where running in traffic is notoriously challenging.

“Huge problems with temperatures for everybody,” he said. “When you start at the back, there is no way you can follow cars closely, or something like that.

"So, there is not much we can do – and I think we lost a big opportunity. So frustration is beyond imagination. But this is the story of the year.”

title: Who is F1’s latest debutant Ryo Hirakawa?
excerpt:
Following a number of Free Practice 1 appearances, Ryo Hirakawa will make his F1 race debut at the Mexico City Grand Prix after Haas announced on Saturday morning that the Japanese racer would replace Esteban Ocon for the remainder of the event. Here is everything you need to know about Formula 1’s latest debutant…

Gaining experience across different categories

After beginning his career by participating in karting championships in his native Japan, Hirakawa graduated to single-seaters in 2010.

From there he progressed through categories including Formula Challenge Japan and the Japanese Formula 3 Championship, winning his debut race in the latter before going on to seal the 2012 title.

Hirakawa’s next step saw him move to Super Formula in 2013, having joined the Toyota Young Driver Program. He would go on to score four wins and four pole positions across his nine years racing in the category.

The Japanese driver also competed in Super GT in the GT500 class between 2014 and 2021, a series in which he won the title in 2017.

World Endurance Championship success

Hirakawa’s racing experience expanded further when he joined the World Endurance Championship in the Hypercar class from 2022 with Toyota Gazoo Racing.

Success quickly followed, as the driver from Japan went on to win the Drivers’ Championship in his maiden season alongside team mates Sebastien Buemi and Brendon Hartley. The squad repeated the feat again in 2023, and also scored a second consecutive 24 Hours of Le Mans triumph.

Hirakawa continues to compete in the series, where the Toyota Racing team are currently leading the 2026 standings.

Arriving into Formula 1

It was announced in September 2023 that Hirakawa had joined the McLaren Driver Development programme and would also become a reserve driver for the outfit. He went on to compete in his maiden FP1 session with the squad at the 2024 Abu Dhabi Grand Prix.

Hirakawa subsequently moved to Alpine for 2025 as a test and reserve driver, with his second FP1 appearance coming at the Japanese Grand Prix – but the now 32-year-old switched to Haas soon afterwards.

This led to four further practice runs in 2025 followed by another two in 2026 – with the second coming just before an unexpected call-up to the main team…

F1’s oldest debutant since 2014

One day after taking the wheel of Ocon’s car during FP1 in Mexico City, Haas released a statement confirming that Hirakawa would replace the Frenchman for the remainder of the weekend.

This makes the Japanese driver the oldest debutant in the sport since Andre Lotterer back in 2014, who was also 32 when he entered the Belgian Grand Prix for what would be his sole F1 event.

Lotterer’s day quickly came to an end when his Caterham suffered a mechanical issue just one lap in – but Hirakawa, who qualified in 19th place for his maiden event, will surely be hoping for better on Sunday in Mexico City.

title: Aston Martin suffer double embarrassment inside first five laps in Mexico City GP
excerpt:
Aston Martin and Honda suffered their latest tale of woe inside the opening few laps of the Mexico City Grand Prix.

On the fifth lap of 71 at the Autodrómo Hermanos Rodríguez, both Fernando Alonso and Lance Stroll were forced to retire.

Alonso, who retired in Q1 on Saturday with a water pressure issue, at least made it back to the garage in his AMR26.

Stroll, though, was forced to pull over on track, sparking a short virtual safety car period.

It is the fifth time this season both Honda-powered Aston Martins have endured a double DNF.

Aston Martin confirmed it had to retire both cars due to "abnormal pressure levels in the PU systems".

title: How Kimi Antonelli can win the F1 title in Mexico City Grand Prix
excerpt:
How Kimi Antonelli can win the title in Mexico City

Kimi Antonelli can win the title in the Mexico City Grand Prix today and be crowned as F1 world champion after missing out in the United States.

The Mercedes driver could have won the title in Austin if he had won the race, George Russell had finished ninth or lower, and Lewis Hamilton had finished fifth or lower.

This was the only combination of results which would have seen Antonelli crowned as F1's youngest-ever world champion - but his ninth victory of the season was coupled with Russell's P8 and Hamilton's P4, meaning Antonelli heads into today's Mexico City race with a 123-point lead over Russell and a 124-point advantage over Hamilton.

After the Austin race, Antonelli has scored 365 points, against 242 for Russell and 241 for Hamilton.

There are 125 points remaining in the season, meaning that to keep their title hopes alive, Russell or Hamilton must win in Mexico City.

If any other driver aside from those two win in Mexico, Antonelli will be champion.

If either of them do, Antonelli would be required to take a P9 finish if Russell wins or a P10 finish if Hamilton wins.

He is still on course to shatter Sebastian Vettel's record as the youngest F1 champion, with the German 23 years, 4 months, 11 days old when he won the 2010 title.

Hamilton starts from pole with Russell and second and Antonelli in fourth. Finishing in that order would be more than enough for Antonelli to seal the title.

Antonelli will now be at least 20 years, 2 months, 7 days old if he wins the title in Mexico, beating Vettel's record by 3 years, 2 months, 4 days.

title: Lewis Hamilton handed vote of confidence ahead of Mexico City GP
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton has been backed to follow up his maiden pole position with Ferrari by claiming victory in the Mexico City Grand Prix.

Hamilton delivered a scintillating second and final lap in Q3 at the Autodrómo Hermanos Rodríguez to clinch the top spot on the grid by just nine thousandths of a second ahead of former Mercedes team-mate George Hamilton.

It was the seven-time F1 champion's first pole since the 2023 Hungarian Grand Prix, whilst at the age of 41, he also became the oldest polesitter since Mario Andretti in the 1982 Italian Grand Prix.

In our latest poll on RacingNews365, we then asked who would win the Mexico City Grand Prix, and Hamilton was a convincing winner, collecting 37.09 per cent of the vote.

From fifth on the grid, after finishing fourth fastest but serving a one-place penalty for his on-track altercation with Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson in second practice on Friday, Max Verstappen emerged as Hamilton's closest challenger with 20.85 per cent.

Verstappen narrowly pipped champion-in-waiting Kimi Antonelli, with the 20-year-old Mercedes driver, who starts fourth, collecting just under 18 per cent.

Third-on-the-grid Charles Leclerc, who appeared favourite for pole before being beaten by team-mate Hamilton, was supported by 12.05 per cent of the voters.

Although George Russell starts alongside Hamilton on the front row, the Mercedes driver only polled 10 per cent.

From sixth and seventh on the grid, McLaren's Lando Norris and Red Bull's Isack Hadjar collected just two per cent of votes between them.

title: George Russell shares honest Kimi Antonelli opinion: 'The truth is...'
excerpt:
George Russell has openly acknowledged that Kimi Antonelli has been operating at a "higher level" this season, insisting their relationship remains strong despite the shifting intra-team dynamics at Mercedes.

Antonelli is on the cusp of clinching his first F1 drivers' championship, needing a mere two points from the Mexico City Grand Prix.

However, coming into the campaign, Russell was the bookmakers' favourite and was widely expected to waltz to the title — even if that diminishes the enormity of claiming motorsport's most illustrious crown.

Nonetheless, it was heavily anticipated — even within the F1 paddock — that the Briton would be coronated at the end of the season, not his significantly less experienced team-mate.

But Antonelli has come on leaps and bounds over the course of the campaign and has dominated large chunks of the schedule.

Although team-mate title-battles often cause internal friction, as they famously did at Mercedes a decade ago with Lewis Hamilton and Nico Rosberg vying for supremacy, Russell is adamant that relations with Antonelli are still good.

"On a personal level, Kimi is obviously a great guy with lots of energy," Russell told media, including RacingNews365.

"We've had no reason this year not to continue a good relationship."

[Article continues below]

Brutal admission from Russell

Recently, reigning champion Lando Norris argued that Antonelli has been "two levels" above Russell, which appears to be something his compatriot agrees with.

The 28-year-old pointed out how few on-track skirmishes he and Antonelli have shared, which he believes has helped keep the partnership healthy.

"I think a lot of these rivalries start because of on-track incidents or actions," Russell added. "The truth is he's been at a higher level than me this year, so we've not really been in that situation too often."

"We've had one or two races, and when it comes to the race itself, we sort of keep ourselves to ourselves and work with our individual engineers to try and get the most out of it."

Russell goes into the 71-lap race at the Autodrómo Hermanos Rodríguez starting second on the grid behind Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton, with Antonelli lining up in fourth.

title: Racing Bulls take advantage of Liam Lawson Mexico City GP disqualification
excerpt:
Racing Bulls has decided to hand Liam Lawson new power unit components for the Mexico City Grand Prix.

The decision comes following Lawson's disqualification from qualifying at the Autodrómo Hermanos Rodríguez for a technical irregularity.

Lawson had qualified a superb eighth for the high-altitude race, although was due to start ninth after being handed a one-place grid penalty following his on-track altercation with Red Bull's four-time F1 champion Max Verstappen in second practice on Friday.

Almost immediately after qualifying, the New Zealander's VCARB 03 was found to have been "in breach of the minimum MGU-K power requirement just after crossing the line on his fastest lap in Q2 at 15:47:36", according to the stewards.

Although Racing Bulls tried to argue Lawson's case, there is rarely, if ever, a defence for a technical breach, leading to the 24-year-old's disqualification.

After later being permitted to start the race, Racing Bulls has opted to fit a new internal combustion engine, turbocharger, exhaust set and ancillary component, all of which exceed the permitted number allowed for the season. The team has also opted to make changes to the suspension set-up.

It means Lawson will now start the race from the pit lane.

title: Liam Lawson handed fiery 'unjust sacking' defence amid F1 uncertainty
excerpt:
Karun Chandhok has offered full-throated support for Liam Lawson keeping his seat at Racing Bulls next season, arguing it would be "one of the most unjust sackings in F1" if he is dropped for Nikola Tsolov.

Lawson had put together a remarkable campaign for the Faenza-based team, and also performed admirably for three rounds at Red Bull when Isack Hadjar was injured.

However, the New Zealander's future in F1 is far from certain, and he is yet to be offered a new contract for next year, with Tsolov fighting to make it to the grid.

The 19-year-old, who is currently second in the F2 drivers' standings, is highly touted and is considered the 'next driver up' in Red Bull's junior programme.

Racing Bulls team principal Alan Permane has admitted the joint, energy drinks-backed team faces a difficult choice, as it grapples with the good problem of having three strong drivers for just two race seats, with Arvid Lindblad widely expected to stay put after an impressive rookie season.

However, Chandhok does not quite see the situation in the same light, with the former F1 driver insistent that Lawson should retain his drive.

"If Liam Lawson gets sacked from this seat, it would be one of the most unjust sackings in F1 because he's done a fantastic job this season," he said on Sky Sports F1 during FP1 in Mexico.

"He's come back carrying the mental baggage of being sacked from the Red Bull top team, went back into the Red Bull seat for three races and did a good job there, and he's delivered really, really well."

Racing Bulls' intrinsic struggle

Chandhok tapped into the inherent conflict within the Racing Bulls team: is it merely there to develop drivers for Red Bull, or does it have its own aims and objectives?

He also suggested there will be a paucity of evidence to suggest that Tsolov will be a better choice than Lawson next season.

He said: As much as I get it, the team is there to prepare drivers for the top team; they are a strong team, they've got their own identity, sponsors and reasons to be competitive, not just to train drivers up to go to the big team...

"I just don't see how they can have any data that suggests that Tsolov is a better option than Liam Lawson. But we'll see."

title: Oliver Bearman confirms Esteban Ocon text amid 'sad' Haas situation
excerpt:
Esteban Ocon was benched by Haas ahead of Saturday's running at the Mexico City Grand Prix.

Oliver Bearman has confirmed that he sent a message to Esteban Ocon after the Frenchman was dropped from the team in Mexico.

Haas announced on Saturday morning in Mexico City that Ocon would be replaced by Ryo Hirakawa for the remainder of the weekend.

The team did not provide a conclusive reason, insisting only that it was not related to illness.

Ocon clarified that there was no incident of physical violence that led to the benching, after a report appeared in the media.

Bearman stated he was unaware of what occurred between the team and Ocon, but revealed he made sure to reach out to his team-mate.

"I sent a message to Esteban," Bearman told media including RacingNews365.

"It's a really tough situation, and I don't know exactly what's happened, if I'm completely honest with you.

"It's never a happy situation when these situations occur."

[Article continues below]

Hirakawa 'very happy' for Hirakawa F1 opportunity

With Ocon sidelined, Hirakawa will make his grand prix debut in unexpected circumstances, and is the oldest rookie to race in F1 since Andre Lotterer in 2014.

The Japanese driver qualified in 18th place, but blamed traffic for missing out on a spot in Q2.

Bearman stated he has been assisting his new stable-mate as much as he can ahead of the race.

"All I can say is that I've been helping Ryo as much as possible to speed up the learning curve.

"It will be a great memory for him and a fantastic experience. But of course in a really challenging and sad circumstance."

When asked what advice he would give Hirakawa for the grand prix, Bearman said: "Send it, send it. Brake at the 50 [metre board] at Turn 1 and go for it."

title: Latest weather update for the 2026 Formula 1 Mexico City Grand Prix
excerpt:
F1 arrives at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez for the Mexico City Grand Prix, with conditions set to put teams' cooling and aerodynamic set-ups to the test.

Sunshine is expected throughout, with air temperatures hovering around 25 degrees. But the stadium section and high altitude of the Mexican circuit mean conditions on track can feel considerably more demanding than the forecast suggests.

The sun index is expected to climb as high as 10, an extreme reading that will heat the asphalt rapidly once the field gets moving.

Partly as a result, track temperatures are forecast to rise to between 40 and 45 degrees by the time the lights go out, a range that typically accelerates tyre degradation and forces teams into earlier pit-stop windows.

A moderate north wind is also forecast across a circuit sitting more than 2,200 metres above sea level, where the thin air already reduces aerodynamic downforce and cools engines less efficiently than at sea level, so any crosswind component adds an extra layer of difficulty.

Drivers could notice the effects most keenly on the long back straight, where cars already run reduced wing levels to compensate for the low air density, and through the fast, sweeping corners where sudden gusts can unsettle the rear of the car mid-corner.

Teams will be monitoring the wind direction closely in the build-up to the race, with set-up choices around wing angle and cooling likely to be fine-tuned right up until late on.

The combination of high track temperatures and a gusting wind is expected to make tyre management and car balance through the stadium section in particular one of the defining factors of the 71-lap race

title: Resurfaced Mexico City GP track adds uncertainty to strategy
excerpt:
Plenty of options are open to the strategists for this race.

Pirelli has identified four viable tyre strategies for the Mexico City Grand Prix, with the recent resurfacing of the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez adding a degree of uncertainty over the best route from lights to flag.

The preferred option for the 71-lap race is likely to be a one-stopper; an approach that involves starting on the medium compound, pitting between laps 35 and 41, and switching to the soft tyre.

An equivalent in Pirelli's simulations is a two-stop alternative that starts on softs, moves to the medium between laps 19 and 25, and returns to the soft tyre for a final stint running from roughly lap 45 to lap 51.

A second one-stop option exists, with drivers starting on soft tyres and switching to the hard compound somewhere between laps 24 and 30.

The final scenario modelled is another two-stopper: soft tyres for the opening 19 to 25 laps, a middle stint on hards lasting until lap 46 to 52, before closing out the race on the medium.

Pirelli has factored an average pit-stop time loss of 22 seconds into its calculations, a figure that will shape how drivers and strategists weigh track position against fresher rubber.

Notably, significant portions of the circuit were resurfaced ahead of this weekend, covering the Turn 16 to Turn 1 section and Turn 7 to Turn 16.

Pirelli head of motorsport business Dario Marrafuschi said the tyre picture remains genuinely open heading into the race.

"There are several possible strategic scenarios for the race, ranging from a one-stop strategy, with more careful tyre management, to a two-stop approach," said Marrafuschi.

[Article continues below]

The circuit's altitude, over 2,200 metres above sea level, strips significant downforce from the cars and increases sliding, which in turn raises the risk of front graining.

Williams' Paul Williams said the new surface was "the biggest unknown for the tyres", adding that "the roughness and grip of the new asphalt will determine both the graining risk and how difficult warm-up proves to be."

After three practice sessions, the teams and drivers will at least have a handle on how best to approach the race, but even then it remains to be seen which strategy will prove the best option.

Marrafuschi added: "The final choice [of strategy] will depend on a range of factors, including each car's characteristics, aerodynamic set-up levels and, above all, the traffic drivers may encounter after a pit stop.

"Many teams may choose to start on the medium and switch to the soft between laps 35 and 41, taking it through to the chequered flag. In this scenario, tyre management will remain an important factor despite the relatively low degradation levels.

"The alternative two-stop strategy would involve starting on the soft, followed by a stint on the medium and a final stint again on the soft. According to our simulations, there is no significant difference in total race time between these two options.

"However, teams opting for the two-stop strategy will need to carefully assess the impact of traffic, as the number of cars they may need to overtake after each stop could prove decisive."

title: Sergio Perez ally makes F1 future prediction after major Cadillac announcement
excerpt:
Carlos Slim Domit, a long-time friend of Sergio Perez, has weighed in on the Mexican driver's F1 future following his renewed commitment with Cadillac.

Slim Domit is the son of Carlos Slim Helu, one of the wealthiest men in the world and the founder of Escuderia Telmex, who funded Perez's junior racing career in Europe in the mid-2000s.

The Slim family remained an avid supporter of Perez throughout his F1 career, which has included stints at Sauber, McLaren, Force India and Red Bull.

Perez has since gone on to become one of the most experienced drivers in F1 history, with his home race in Mexico today set to be his 300th start, making him only the seventh driver to ever reach that milestone.

The 36-year-old sat out the 2025 campaign after his exit from Red Bull, but was quickly snapped up by Cadillac, who saw his experience as a valuable asset for its debut season.

Speaking exclusively to RacingNews365, Slim Domit voiced his joy at seeing Perez back competing in F1 full-time.

"It was a big challenge, a lot of work to make this happen," he said.

"He's a driver so complete today; he's a driver who is still very fast. He's very committed.

"He wants to consolidate his career, after all the many things that he has done, to develop, to commit, to develop a new team such as Cadillac.

"He's at a very good stage. We all, as fans, wanted him back, and now we have the chance to see him competing again at the Mexican Grand Prix.

"And very specially, as a coincidence, it's his 300th grand prix, happening in his home [country]."

[Article continues below]

Perez F1 future will not be dicated by 'age or physical issues'

Ahead of Perez's home event, Cadillac announced that Perez would remain at the team until at least the end of the 2029 season.

At that stage of his career, Perez will be 39 years old, but Slim insisted that it is not a factor that will be an issue for Mexico's most successful driver.

"I think it will depend on him. Physically and mentally, he can go for a long time. But it will depend on him.

"He also wants to be very close to his family; always, when he's with the team, he's 100 per cent focused.

"It will depend more on him than on age or physical issues.

"I'm very proud to be his friend and to have lived with him through this tough career that we've experienced together.

"Watching firsthand the sacrifices that he had to make to be here, the huge work that he has committed to doing, and his mantra: he is really a person who has never given up.

"He lost his seat many times, with no bright future ahead, and he never gave up, and that's the picture of his career."

title: Esteban Ocon scolded after Haas F1 benching: 'That frustrates me'
excerpt:
2009 F1 champion Jenson Button has admitted he is “frustrated” by the situation revolving around Esteban Ocon, suggesting he may have thrown away the rest of his F1 career.

Haas confirmed at the end of September that Ocon would depart the team at the end of the 2026 campaign, bringing an end to his two-year stint.

Shortly after, Haas confirmed it had signed rookie Rafael Camara, who is expected to partner Oliver Bearman.

Button has acknowledged that such a situation would have been difficult for Ocon to swallow.

“It's always difficult for a driver when you know that your team is looking at someone else for the following year, and you're out,” Button told Sky F1.

However, on Saturday morning in Mexico City, the team confirmed that Ocon would be replaced for the rest of the race weekend, with Ryo Hirakawa stepping in for the Frenchman.

Haas gave no official reason behind the withdrawal, but clarified that it did not have to do with illness.

Reports emerged that Ocon may have been involved in a physical altercation with team principal Ayao Komatsu, a story that the grand prix winner denied.

But there was some tension brewing, with Ocon voicing his displeasure over team radio during FP2 over the team's plan to run him on the medium compound, when he desired the soft.

Button has hypothesised that Ocon may have thrown away his F1 career over the matter.

“The best thing for him to do for number one, which is himself, is to drive as hard as he can, work as hard as he can, and show how good he is.

“He can't do that anymore because of a disagreement on tyres in practice.

“It's not even qualifying or the race; it's practice. That frustrates me when I see that.

“These are 22 of the best drivers in the world who don't get this opportunity easily, and he's possibly just thrown away the rest of his career in F1.”

title: Lando Norris shocked after comparison to F1 rivals: 'It baffles me'
excerpt:
Lando Norris has stated he is "baffled" that McLaren can produce strong lap times on occasion after comparing his car to others on the F1 grid.

Norris ended qualifying in Mexico City in sixth place, three-tenths of a second down on pole-sitter Lewis Hamilton.

However, team-mate Oscar Piastri endured a more challenging time behind the wheel and suffered a shock early exit in Q2.

Having enjoyed a strong surge in form around the summer break period, McLaren has since slipped back in the order and is without a podium in the last four grands prix.

Norris has stated for some time that his McLaren car is too unpredictable when it comes to single-lap performance, a trait that was evident once again this weekend.

"We're just not quick enough, the car's too difficult to drive," Norris told media including RacingNews365.

"Maybe one in 50 I can put together, and everyone says, 'Oh, you've got a good car.'

"But it's not true. My Q2 lap, I just had an amazing headwind in Turn 12, gained one and a half tenths, just because the car brakes.

"The next half, I try and go the same speed in, I lose the rear, I lose a tenth, so I got a two and a half tenths delta to my previous.

"It's just too difficult, especially when it's like the onboards from others. It baffles me how we can be quick sometimes."

[Article continues below]

Norris knew he was 'screwed' in Q3

Norris pointed to the struggles endured by Piastri in qualifying as an indicator of how difficult it is to put a lap together.

"I don't think anything slipped away, just the lap I did was pretty phenomenal in the car that we have," he said.

"It shows where Oscar is and the struggles we've been having, how difficult it is to put a lap together in this car."

While sixth on the grid marks one of Norris' lowest starting positions of the season, the reigning champion voiced satisfaction with the effort, as he pre-empted that he would be “skrewed” in Q3.

"So I'm pretty happy with a P6, honestly. You never really know what you're going to get.

"After I did a good lap in Q2, I knew I was screwed for Q3 because the chance of me repeating that lap was impossible.

"It's just that we're too slow. Every now and then, I can put a magical lap together, and everyone has a bit of hope, which is not a good thing because then we see the reality in Q3."

title: Kimi Antonelli shares details of Mexico illness as title history awaits
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli has been operating while under the weather this weekend in Mexico City.

Kimi Antonelli has opened up about the illness he has been suffering from throughout the Mexico City Grand Prix weekend.

In the build-up to the race weekend, the Italian was excused from media duties on Thursday as he focused on getting himself ready for driving.

Antonelli sits on the verge of winning his maiden F1 title this weekend, needing only a ninth-place result on Sunday to become the youngest champion in the sport's history.

However, the weekend has not been up to par with his usual standards on display this year, as he revealed he is still suffering from an ailment.

When asked how bad his condition was on Thursday, Antonelli told media including RacingNews365: “Very bad.

“I had high fever and stomach problems, so it hasn't been easy. Now I feel okay. Just low in energy.

“Just feeling pretty tired, so it's going to be important to try and sleep well because I haven't been sleeping well in these days.

“Hopefully tomorrow I will have more energy.”

Antonelli keen to avoid chaos at 'tricky' Turn 1

Antonelli ended qualifying on Saturday in fifth place, but will be bumped up one position on the starting grid due to a penalty for Max Verstappen.

With the run to Turn 1 from the starting grid being the longest of the season, there is an opportunity for Antonelli to make up positions from the second row of the grid.

While it's a possibility he is aware of, Antonelli highlighted his desire is to get through the opening corner safely as he hopes to close out the title fight.

“It's a long run into Turn 1, so it's just going to be important to get off the line well,” he said.

“Hopefully, we can gain a couple of places. Of course, we'll have to stay out of trouble as well because Turn 1 is always very tricky.

“If we get a good start, we have a good chance to then move forward. The race pace is still not as strong as Ferrari, but I think we can still do well.”

title: Lewis Hamilton facing 'guesstimate' for Mexico City GP after practice pain
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton has suggested he is on the back foot heading into the Mexico City Grand Prix as he targets his second race victory of the season.

The seven-time champion prevailed on Saturday in qualifying, besting former team-mate George Russell to the top of the timesheet.

It marked Hamilton's first pole position in over three years, and his first with the Ferrari team.

But while he was able to showcase strong pace over a single lap, Hamilton is less confident about his prospects for the race due to a lack of running in practice.

Hamilton was forced to pull to the side of the track during FP2 with a power unit issue, which he feels has hindered his preparation for the race.

"In general, I don't think this year I've had a good long run," Hamilton told media including RacingNews365.

"We've either pushed our short laps too long and then got into the long run, but I've not had one good long run where it's consistent and got the balance right.

"Coming into this weekend, we met up on Wednesday. We went over all the areas that we can improve on, different approaches, things that we learned from the last race.

"We're like, 'We're going to make sure we get a good long run in this weekend.' Big, big focus. And then the car stopped!"

Hamilton under pressure to keep hold of P1

Having missed out on the long runs in FP2, Hamilton is unsure what configurations he needs for the race.

The 41-year-old stated he will "guess" heading into the grand prix as he seeks his second win with Ferrari.

"I just watched the rest of the session where everyone was pounding around and getting those long runs in.

"I don't know how the car will behave on the long run on heavy fuel, and I also don't know the settings that I'm going to need.

"So those are the things I'm going to have to kind of guesstimate tonight and take my... we'll take our best guess to hopefully get the car in the right window for tomorrow.

"Very, very challenging. It's obviously a really long way down to Turn 1."

title: Max Verstappen voices Lando Norris frustration after Mexico qualifying incident
excerpt:
Max Verstappen had to settle for fourth place during qualifying in Mexico and was not happy with the traffic he encountered during the session.

Max Verstappen has voiced his frustration after feeling his final lap in qualifying in Mexico was hindered by Lando Norris.

Verstappen entered the session with a one-place grid penalty hanging over his head due to a clash in practice with Liam Lawson.

It meant it was impossible for the Dutchman to walk away from pole position in hand, however Verstappen was still involved in the fight for the fastest lap of the session.

As he ended his final attempt in Q3, Verstappen encountered traffic as he entered the stadium section of the Autodromo Hermanos Rodriquez, and locked up into Turn 13.

Verstappen insisted he would have been in contention for the fastest lap of qualifying if Norris had placed his car elsewhere when letting him through.

“I had two cars in front of me, so I was already losing downforce in Turn 12,” Verstappen told Viaplay.

“It just broke out more there, because that car was only one and a half to two seconds ahead of me.

“And then he [Norris] parks it on the right side, which is exactly where you want to open up for the hairpin."

“You can’t position your car properly, and you also lose your reference point on the right side.

“It’s a shame. Of course, pole position was within reach. Then we would have been second.”

Driver

Verstappen happier with Red Bull balance

Having had his frustrations with the Red Bull car at times this year, Verstappen at least was more content with the RB22's handling this time around.

“Fortunately, the car is a lot better. The whole weekend was bad, but in qualifying the car was better.

“In qualifying, we made quite a few changes to the car. It just felt much better, because I wasn’t at all satisfied in practice.

“The car was very difficult to drive, it just didn’t have a good balance, but in qualifying it was just okay.”

However, it is still not without its limitations in Mexico City.

“Of course, we have certain issues with the car over the kerbs.

“That’s not going entirely well, but after Q1 we were right in the mix the whole time. In that area, I think we’ve made some progress.

“On the final lap, everything just came together really well. It’s just that sometimes you have a bit of bad luck."

title: FIA issued 'calm down' warning before ill-tempered Verstappen-Lawson clash
excerpt:
Karun Chandhok has revealed that the FIA explicitly told team principals to rein in their drivers during free practice hours before Max Verstappen and Liam Lawson collided in FP2 at the Mexico City Grand Prix.

The two collided at Turn 14 when Verstappen, who had gone off the edge of the track, rejoined and made contact with Lawson's front wing, triggering a red flag at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez.

Both drivers were subsequently handed a one-place grid penalty and a penalty point.

Speaking on Sky Sports F1, Chandhok explained the chain of events that led to the clash.

"Now we heard his [Max's] engineer telling him to get ahead of Liam, to get track position ahead of Liam... So that's what Max is trying to do," he said.

"When they get down to this hairpin, Liam has clearly decided he's in no mood to let Max pass. So he comes back down the inside... And I think this has annoyed Max because he thought, 'Well, I'm now in front. You should get out of the way.' Max opts to go beyond the edge of the track... and then sort of just barges into Liam as they come through the right-hander.

"So, the whole thing, in my opinion, just feels a bit unnecessary and a bit clumsy for FP2."

Stewards' warning

Chandhok went on to reveal that stewards had gathered all 11 team bosses that same morning to issue a direct warning over driver conduct in practice sessions.

He also referred to the Esteban Ocon flashpoint that ultimately culminated in the Frenchman being stood down for the weekend at Haas, after a disagreement that stemmed from when the Haas driver vented his frustration over team radio to race engineer Laura Mueller after his run plan was switched from soft to medium tyres.

Haas subsequently withdrew Ocon from the remainder of the weekend, with reserve driver Ryo Hirakawa stepping in, though the team has offered no formal explanation for the decision beyond confirming it was not due to illness.

"I get that in Esteban Ocon's situation, you're trying to get information, you're trying to do the learning, but there's got to be a time and place for this level of aggression," Chandhok added.

"Now, the reason I should point out why they have been penalised. Because in the past we've seen drivers not be penalised for free practice incidents.

"But [on Friday] morning, all of the team managers, 11 team managers, were in a meeting with the stewards, who told them, 'Ask your drivers to behave in free practice.'

"We've seen a few too many incidents in the recent races; we saw Leclerc and George, for example, in Austin, and the stewards have said, 'Look, we're going to start penalising people if they don't behave in free practice.'

"And I think that's why both of these drivers have got that one-place penalty. And really, they both played a part in the way that played out. Although you could say, Max went off the track and barged into him there..."

title: MotoGP manufacturer confirms sensational withdrawal from Qatar round
excerpt:
The conflict in the Middle East has seen one MotoGP manufacturer pull out of the upcoming round from Qatar.

Yamaha has confirmed it will not take part in the 2026 Qatar Grand Prix, citing "company-wide travel restrictions" linked to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East.

The manufacturer issued a statement revealing it has informed MotoGP it does not intend to run its four bikes at the Lusail circuit, with concerns mounting over a potential escalation in the USA-Iran war.

"Following its latest assessment of the situation in the Middle East, Yamaha has not identified sufficient grounds to change its existing company-wide travel restrictions," the statement read.

"As a result, Yamaha has informed MotoGP Group about its decision not to participate in the 2026 Qatar Grand Prix.

"This decision reflects Yamaha's assessment of the information currently available and is independent of the measures implemented by MotoGP Group and the event organiser.

"Yamaha remains fully committed to MotoGP and looks forward to returning to competition at the Portuguese Grand Prix."

The statement does not mention specific teams by name, but it is understood to apply to Yamaha's factory outfit as well as partner squad Pramac.

MotoGP warns of 'consequences' after Yamaha withdrawal

MotoGP has issued a response to the news, stating that the non-participation from Yamaha will likely result in 'sporting implications'.

“MotoGP is disappointed by Yamaha's decision not to participate in the Qatar Grand Prix,” it said.

“While we recognise the team is subject to a broader corporate policy restricting travel to the Middle East, we do not believe this decision reflects the extensive assurances provided to all championship stakeholders.

“Following consultation with the State of Qatar, Lusail International Circuit, independent safety advisers and MotoGP's own ongoing risk assessment process, MotoGP has not received any information that would warrant a change to the current plans for the event.

“We communicated that position, together with the latest available information, to all Manufacturers and Teams today and welcome the confirmation from the remainder of the grid that they will compete in Qatar, and we thank them for that commitment.

“In addition to the contractual implications of Yamaha's decision for its agreements with MotoGP and IRTA, Yamaha's non-participation also carries sporting implications, with any sporting consequences to be managed by the FIM in accordance with the Championship regulations.”
